transcript:
Meeting: Redwood Edgecases Demo: long context, high TPS, streaming backpressure & timeouts
Date/Time: 2026-12-18 15:00 UTC
Duration: 42 minutes
Attendees: Samir Patel (Redwood AE), Priya Mehta (Redwood SE), Luca Chen (Redwood CSM), Lena Ortiz (Nimbus Health - CTO), Marco Ruiz (Nimbus - SRE), Anya Singh (Nimbus - Lead ML)

Summary:
- Walkthrough of Redwood API, Console, and Optimize focused on edge cases: very long context (>50k tokens), sustained high TPS, streaming backpressure handling, and timeout/retry behavior.
- Discussed hosted vs dedicated vs private (VPC) tradeoffs for Nimbus Health (regulated healthcare).
- Agreed on a small pilot: 1-week benchmark with specific load script and long-context prompt set.

Topics Covered:
- Long context pipeline and KV cache behavior
- Model variants for quantization and cost lift
- Streaming (SSE / websocket) backpressure and client window sizing
- Idle/request timeouts and retry semantics
- Monitoring: token-level cost, latency p95/p99, per-route traces
- Security: SOC2, SAML, KMS/HSM, audit logs, data residency

Action Items (recap at end): Samir to send pricing; Priya to send load script; Customer to share traces and prompt sets.

--- Transcript ---
[00:00] Samir (Redwood): Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick intro, I'm Samir on the AE side, with Priya our SE and Luca from CSM.
[00:08] Lena (Customer): Hi, thanks. I'll jump in quick — priority for us is privacy and predictable costs, we're in healthcare so PHI comes up.
[00:15] Marco: Yeah hi, Marco here. We run a patient triage flow that needs long context — like full visit notes — and also we push a lot of short requests when ingesting messages, so both long context and high TPS.
[00:26] Priya (Redwood SE): Great, that's exactly what we wanted to show. Today we'll demo three things: how Redwood handles long contexts (50k+ tokens), then sustained high TPS load and finally streaming behavior with backpressure and timeouts. We'll call out tradeoffs between Hosted, Dedicated, and Private (VPC).
[00:40] Anya (Customer): Quick Q — do you support customer KMS in hosted mode? We need CMK for encryption at rest.
[00:47] Samir: Short answer: yes, we integrate with customer KMS/HSM in our Private deployment and we have envelope encryption for hosted with customer-managed keys on request. We'll follow up with the security pack.
[00:58] Priya: Ok jumping into the Console. (screen-share noises) So here's a long-context job; under the hood we keep a KV cache to avoid recomputing prefixes. Note the cache hit-rate metric here — when you keep repeated patient history, you get big savings.
[01:15] Marco: When you say KV cache, is that the "K V cash" thing — I've seen notes where transcription shows it oddly, is it persisted across requests or per-session?
[01:24] Priya: Haha yeah Fireflies loves to call it K V cash. It's per-route and per-model policy; you can choose session-scoped or cross-session prefix cache. For PHI we recommend session-scoped and TTLs.
[01:36] [01:36] Priya: For 50k token contexts we push a streaming approach: we chunk the context, warm the KV cache, and then stream generation. On the model side we use quantized variants to reduce memory overhead — that reduces cost but you'd want to validate quality.
[01:50] Lena: What's the latency like for a full 50k context generation? Our SLA target is p95 < 1.2s for short responses, and for long-form summarization maybe p95 < 8s — is that realistic?
[02:02] Priya: So it depends on tokens generated. For a large summarize call over 50k context, end-to-end may hit several seconds. In our Dedicated configs we've seen 5-8s for common model variants; hosted depends on burst capacity. We'll include benchmark numbers.
[02:18] Marco: For our ingestion pipeline we need sustained 3k RPS of small requests (single-turn, 30-60 tokens) — can Redwood hit that?
[02:27] Samir: Yes, with Dedicated reserved pools and batching you can hit several thousand RPS. We intelligently batch small requests; downside is potential added batching latency, but we can configure latency SLOs and autoscale.
[02:39] Anya: How do you handle backpressure for streaming? We use WebSockets and clients can get overwhelmed.
[02:45] Priya: Good question. Our streaming uses chunked responses over websockets/SSE and we expose a flow-control window. If the client can't keep up, the server will buffer up to a threshold then apply backpressure — we can drop to lower-fidelity model variants or pause generation. We also support client ACKs for chunks.
[03:02] Marco: Is that configurable per-route? We need different behavior for triage vs bulk export.
[03:07] Priya: Yes, per-route policies. You can set buffer size, client window, fallback model, and timeout thresholds.
[03:13] Lena: Timeout semantics — if a stream stalls for say 30s during live summarization, do you close or retry? What about duplicate events?
[03:20] Priya: We have two timeouts: idle timeout and request timeout. Idle default is 30s, request timeout default can be 120s. If idle triggers, the server will close the stream and mark the request as aborted; our SDKs surface a retry token so clients can resume or retry idempotently depending on your design. For dedupe we recommend idempotency keys.
[03:37] Samir: Also we capture partial outputs in the Console and you can configure automatic fallback to completion-mode generation if streaming fails.
[03:44] Marco: Any observed behavior under sustained high TPS that causes timeouts? e.g., queueing that pushes requests over request-timeout?
[03:50] Priya: Under extreme load, if all GPUs are saturated you can see queueing, which is why Dedicated capacity with autoscale and burst is recommended. We also have smart routing to route to cheaper model variants or cross-region fallback to avoid timeouts.
[04:05] Anya: Can you show the load test you mentioned earlier?
[04:08] Priya: Sure — quick demo. (typing) This is our load script; we simulate 3k RPS of 40-token requests for 10 minutes with a steady ramp. We'll instrument p50/p95/p99 and token cost.
[04:21] [04:21] Priya: Running now... you can see we maintain p95 ~120ms, p99 ~300ms in this Dedicated pool; when I artificially reduce pool capacity you'll see p99 spike and some requests hit request-timeout.
[04:36] Marco: Do you have sample configs for client-side backpressure? We currently have a fragile websocket consumer that re-opens on every error.
[04:42] Priya: Yes, we have an SDK snippet that implements a sliding window + ACKs and exponential backoff for retries; I'll include that in the benchmark repo we share.
[04:51] Lena: On security: SOC2 is a must; also we need SAML SSO and RBAC across teams. Is audit logging per-token available?
[04:59] Samir: We provide audit logs with request metadata. Token-level content logging is optional and can be disabled; for PHI you can opt for no content storage and integrative KMS. SAML/SSO and RBAC are supported in Private and Dedicated with enterprise packages.
[05:13] Anya: For telemetry, can the Console surface per-route token cost breakdown? We need to allocate billing to products.
[05:19] Luca (CSM): Yes, Console has token-level cost breakout by route/model and you can tag routes for chargeback. We'll share a screenshot.
[05:27] Marco: A couple of edge questions: 1) If we do long context plus streaming, does the KV cache warm cause an initial latency spike? 2) What happens when the client disconnects mid-stream — do you keep computed KV objects?
[05:37] Priya: 1) Yes, warm-up can add an initial spike; we mitigate by pre-warming the KV cache asynchronously or by sending a warm-up request. 2) If the client disconnects mid-stream we keep the KV entries depending on TTL and cache policy; for PHI-sensitive flows set short TTLs and session-scoped caches so nothing persists longer than needed.
[05:55] Samir: For pilot scope, we propose three scenarios: A) long-context summarize (50k tokens) single concurrent request, B) sustained small requests at target TPS (3k RPS), C) mixed streaming where 10% of calls are streaming heavy and we enforce backpressure.
[06:10] Lena: Ok sounds good. Rough budget — what's the expected cost delta for hosted vs dedicated for our mix?
[06:16] Samir: Hosted is simpler but per-token may be higher for sustained loads. Dedicated with reserved capacity amortizes GPUs; for your TPS and long-context usage I expect Dedicated will be 30-50% cheaper at scale, but we will run concrete estimates in the pilot.
[06:30] Marco: Does Dedicated require us to manage any infra? We want minimal ops.
[06:34] Priya: No, Redwood manages the serving runtime for Dedicated; you get reserved pools and we handle autoscale. Private (VPC/on-prem) requires more customer involvement but gives you full control and data plane in your network.
[06:48] Anya: Any limitations on model variants for long-context/quantization? We worry about hallucinations if quantized too aggressively.
[06:55] Priya: Right — quantization can impact quality. We recommend model A-quant1 for inference where quality-impact is low, but we'll run evals tied to your prompt sets in the pilot to track ROUGE/accuracy/regression alerts using Redwood Optimize.
[07:10] Lena: If streaming timeouts happen during a patient triage, that's sensitive. What's your recommended retry/backoff approach for idempotency?
[07:17] Priya: For triage we recommend idempotency + server-side partial transcript persist so you can resume and dedupe. Also set request-timeout higher for critical flows and prefer Dedicated so queueing-induced timeouts are reduced.
[07:30] Marco: Are there any published runbooks? We've seen sample docs for backpressure, but need step-by-step for our SREs.
[07:36] Samir: Yes — we'll share the SRE runbook and a sample k8s/EKS deployment for Private. Also include recommended autoscale policies.
[07:45] Anya: On metrics — what traces do you capture? We need correlation IDs and per-token timings for debugging.
[07:51] Priya: We emit per-request traces, token emission times, model layer timings, and we support OpenTelemetry export. We'll show a sample trace later.
[07:59] [08:00] (Demo continues — Priya shows Console views and a live streaming session where the client window is artificially limited)
[08:12] Priya: See here — when client window is small, chunks queue up and you can see buffer size climb; after threshold we hit backpressure and seed a fallback to a lower-fidelity model.
[08:25] Marco: Is fallback seamless or does it change response format? We depend on structured JSON output.
[08:30] Priya: Fallback keeps output schema consistent; you can configure to maintain structured fields or return a flag that quality may be degraded.
[08:39] Lena: About telemetry retention — we can't keep PHI logs beyond 90 days in our region. Can retention be configured?
[08:45] Samir: Yes retention windows are configurable, and for Private you can keep logs in your own S3 with your lifecycle policies.
[08:54] Marco: Any limits on request size for streaming? We deal with 100k token contexts occasionally.
[08:59] Priya: We support large contexts via chunking and KV, but practical limits depend on model and memory. For 100k we'd recommend Private with multi-GPU sharding or a model with extended context support. We'll include guidance in the doc.
[09:13] Anya: What's your SLO for streaming reliability?
[09:16] Luca: For Dedicated enterprise customers we offer uptime SLAs and target p99 streaming reliability > 99.9% — specific numbers will be in the contract.
[09:25] Marco: For the pilot, can we try a host that simulates our worst-case: 100 concurrent long-context streams + 3k RPS of short calls?
[09:32] Priya: Yes, that's within scope. We'll design the load script to ramp and include sudden spikes to trigger backpressure behavior.
[09:40] Samir: Ok quick recap of next steps — we'll send the pilot proposal and pricing, Priya will push the benchmark repo and sample SDK snippets, Nimbus will provide prompt sets and traces.
[09:50] Lena: One thing — on paperwork we'll need an NDA + security addendum before we share PHI examples.
[09:56] Samir: Understood — we'll route an NDA via legal and include an addendum.
[10:00] Marco: Last Q — if we do Dedicated, is there a path to Private later with minimal migration risk?
[10:06] Priya: Yes we design artifacts to be portable; model artifacts, prompts, and route configs are exportable. Migration path is a supported engagement.
[10:14] Luca: I'll open the pilot opportunity in CRM and include the scope items.
[10:20] Samir: Thanks all — we'll follow up with the docs and schedule kickoff.

(End of recording)
